metadata.file_name: 216. Delpatro (2026). Effects of COVID-19 education policies on students’ learning proficiency in Latin America—Insights from PISA 2022.pdf
metadata.title: Effects of COVID-19 education policies on students’ learning proficiency in Latin America—Insights from PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries and constructs student-level binary outcomes based on whether the student’s average across the 10 plausible values exceeds the PISA Level 2 threshold in math and reading. The analytic sample is restricted to schools closed due to the pandemic (including cases where the school closure variable is missing), and then merged student and school questionnaires to form a working dataset of 55,041 observations. The manuscript reports “weighted” and “unweighted” versions of ML evaluation metrics, but it does not name the specific PISA weight variable(s) used in the weighted analyses; therefore the exact weight variable cannot be extracted. Missing covariates are imputed using KNN (k=7) before model training, and the ML models are evaluated with a holdout test set and GroupKFold by school/country to reduce information leakage across the nested sampling structure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Start from PISA 2022 student microdata for 11 LAC countries; exclude Costa Rica because ESCS is completely missing (6113 observations), and exclude remaining observations with missing ESCS, leaving 71,375 observations. Keep a set of student/family covariates (Table 1) and merge with school questionnaire data (Tables 2–3). Restrict the working sample to schools closed due to the pandemic; the school-closure restriction yields 55,041 observations and 2,358 schools. The restriction also includes cases where the school day closure variable is missing (7,259 student observations). After restriction, retain 70 covariates (some omitted due to irrelevance or high missingness), then impute missing covariate values using KNN imputation (k=7) for the small proportion of missing data.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teachers have time to integrate devices
Resources to support teachers remote learning

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (age 15) — Latin America & Caribbean — Math proficiency (Level 2+ threshold)
main_findings.target_variable: Math proficiency (Level 2 or above; binary from averaged PVs)
top_predictors: Resources to support teachers remote learning (CEP2)
Teacher communication with students and parents (CEP3)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Gradient boosted trees via XGBoost. Weighted metrics (holdout): AUROC 0.8627, APRC 0.7261, ACC 0.8145, BACC 0.7503, F1 0.6474, MCC 0.5252. Unweighted: AUROC 0.8829, APRC 0.7707, ACC 0.8222, BACC 0.7713, F1 0.6846, MCC 0.5636. Validation: 5-fold CV with hyperparameter tuning using AUROC; holdout test set; GroupKFold by school/country used for leakage control.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 data for 10 Latin American countries restricted to pandemic-closed schools, the study leveraged CEP1–CEP3 (and their interactions with Number of days school closed), together with Family SES (index), to predict Math proficiency (Level 2 or above; binary from averaged PVs), finding that policy effects are strongly non-linear and depend on closure duration, with negative associations for teacher communication at high closure levels and positive associations for student/teacher resource supports at medium-to-high investment ranges. This indicates that sustaining learning during prolonged shutdowns requires aligning remote-learning resource intensity with closure length, and that teacher communication alone may not buffer learning losses for extended closures.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (age 15) — Latin America & Caribbean — Reading proficiency (Level 2+ threshold)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading proficiency (Level 2 or above; binary from averaged PVs)
top_predictors: Resources to support teachers remote learning (CEP2)
Teacher communication with students and parents (CEP3)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Gradient boosted trees via XGBoost. Weighted metrics (holdout): AUROC 0.8497, APRC 0.8586, ACC 0.7641, BACC 0.7644, F1 0.7685, MCC 0.5284. Unweighted: AUROC 0.8690, APRC 0.8692, ACC 0.7817, BACC 0.7817, F1 0.7837, MCC 0.5634. Validation: 5-fold CV with AUROC-based grid search; holdout test set; GroupKFold by school/country for leakage control.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 data for 10 Latin American countries restricted to pandemic-closed schools, the study leveraged CEP1–CEP3 (and their interactions with Number of days school closed), together with Family support for education, to predict Reading proficiency (Level 2 or above; binary from averaged PVs), finding that reading-policy relationships also show non-linear patterns with closure duration but that student resources (CEP1) are comparatively more effective at higher closure levels than teacher communication. This indicates that policy packages emphasizing student learning materials and home-support enabling conditions may be more effective for protecting reading competencies during long school shutdowns, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional associations.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 microdata for 10 Latin American countries, restricting the sample to schools closed due to COVID-19 and predicting whether students reach PISA Level 2+ in math and reading (binary outcomes derived by averaging the 10 plausible values and applying the Level 2 thresholds). Three ML classifiers are compared—logistic regression, neural networks, and gradient boosted trees (XGBoost)—with XGBoost selected as best-performing using AUROC in grid search and evaluated on a holdout test set with additional metrics (AUROC, APRC, ACC, BACC, F1, MCC). For math, weighted AUROC is 0.8627 and for reading weighted AUROC is 0.8497, with consistently higher performance for XGBoost across whole and sub-samples. The paper uses SHAP (TreeExplainer) to interpret non-linear and interaction effects between COVID-19 policy intensity and school closure duration, but the authors explicitly frame results as correlational (no causal claims). A key limitation is that the manuscript does not report the exact PISA weight variable name used in “weighted” ML evaluation, and SHAP-based importance is not equivalent to causal impact.
